chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Khalid ibn Nafi' al-Bajali from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who granted another man the right to reside in his house for the duration of the owner's life. The one who granted the residence died, and the one who was granted it remained. I said: Do you see if the heirs wish to evict him, is it for them to do so? He said: I see that the house should be valued at a fair price, and one should look to one-third of the deceased's estate. If there is in his one-third enough to cover the price of the house, then the heirs cannot evict him. And if the one-third is not enough to cover the price of the house, then they can evict him.

It was said to him: Do you see if the man who was granted the residence dies after the death of the owner of the house, does the residence belong to the heirs of the one who was granted it? He said: No.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What this report contained from his saying 'meaning the owner of the house' when he mentioned that a man granted a man residence in his house, is indeed an error from the narrator and a misconception from him in the interpretation, because the rulings he mentioned afterwards are only valid if he had granted the residence for the life of the one to whom it was granted. At that time, it is valued and considered with regard to the one-third, its increase and decrease. And if the matter were as the interpreter of the hadith mentioned, that he granted it for the duration of his (the grantor's) life, then when he died, the residence would be voided, and there would be no need for him to value it and consider it with the one-third. And we have clarified what indicates that.

ai.seo_question: What happens to a right of residence granted for the owner's life when the owner dies?
ai.summary: This ruling from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the inheritance implications of a life estate (*sukna*), establishing that heirs' right to evict depends on whether the deceased's one-third share covers the property's valuation. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) provides a nuanced distinction based on whether the duration was tied to the grantor's or grantee's life, a point refined by the commentator's correction of a likely narrational ambiguity. This highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on precise textual interpretation (*ta'wil*) in resolving practical property disputes.
